stories.title: Skanska Promotes Tom Leptich, Albert Martin to New Roles in Seattle
stories.excerpt: Skanska has promoted Tom Leptich to Vice President of Operations, and Albert Martin to Vice President and Account Manager for its Skanska USA Building operations across the Puget Sound region and the Inland Northwest. Each has spent more than two decades with the company. As vice president of operations, Leptich will oversee project execution and field operations across Washington. Since joining Skanska in 2000, Leptich has demonstrated a strong commitment to operational excellence, developing people, and delivering successful project outcomes. As vice president and account manager, Martin will continue his focus on building Skanska’s K-12 market, as well as strengthening and expanding client relationships and identifying new business opportunities. During his career, Martin has led large projects across the education, civic, healthcare, and commercial sectors that have positively impacted communities throughout Washington. The two promotions are the latest in a series from within the Seattle office. The post Skanska Promotes Tom Leptich, Albert Martin to New Roles in Seattle appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Skanska promotes Leptich to VP operations, Martin to VP account manager in Seattle.
Leadership continuity: both executives have 20+ years tenure at Skanska.
Focus expands on K-12 education and commercial sectors across Puget Sound and Inland Northwest.
stories.summary: Skanska USA Building elevated two long-tenured executives within its Seattle regional office. Tom Leptich becomes VP of operations overseeing project execution across Washington; Albert Martin moves to VP and account manager with emphasis on K-12 market expansion. Both promotions signal stability and internal development focus within the Pacific Northwest construction and development pipeline.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily. Promotions in commercial and education construction suggest Skanska's Seattle office is active and well-capitalized, which may indicate competitive pressure on general contracting costs for apartment projects in the Puget Sound region, but does not signal material changes to demand, supply, or financing.

stories.title: Pinnacle Group Sells Rights to Upper West Side Apartment Tower for $88M
stories.excerpt: Pinnacle Group has offloaded another asset, this time on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. The prominent New York City landlord, which put a massive rent-stabilized portfolio into bankruptcy last year, sold its rights to an apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to private real estate company Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The Real Deal first reported the sale, citing filings by Pinnacle’s parent company, Zarasai Group, with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The filings, dated Aug. 13, announced the successfully completed sale of Pinnacle’s 100 percent interest in the 15-story building’s lease rights and a 50 percent hold on the land rights. Daniel Parker, Gary Phillips and Will Silverman at Eastdil Secured Savills advised on the deal. An $11 million surplus from the sale is slated to be deposited into the account of Series C bondholders. A spokesperson for Pinnacle Group could not be reached for comment on the most recent sale. The property carried an existing loan balance of about $65 million as of late March, last transferred from Starwood Mortgage Capital to a Barclays-sponsored commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) trust in 2023. Pinnacle secured the leasehold to 323 West 96th Street in 2007, according to city records, and paid another $27 million for its land rights stake in 2016. The 173-unit apartment building, built in 2001, sits at the corner of East 96th Street and First Avenue. The sale comes days after news that Pinnacle offloaded a $128 million condominium and commercial portfolio spanning 39 transactions across Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan. The buyer was Friar Park JW, an entity with links to Tremada Holdings, an affiliate of London-based property company William Pears Group. Pinnacle, led by Joel Wiener, placed a portfolio of roughly 5,000 rent-stabilized apartments across New York City into bankruptcy in May 2025 after facing approximately $574.4 million in debt. Summit Properties
bullets: Pinnacle Group sold 323 West 96th Street Upper West Side apartment rights to Lightstone for $88M.
Pinnacle offloaded rent-stabilized portfolio amid bankruptcy; $11M surplus flows to Series C bondholders.
Sale price $88M against $65M existing loan; distressed asset cycling to new operator.
stories.summary: Pinnacle Group, which filed bankruptcy on a large rent-stabilized portfolio last year, sold its leasehold and 50% land interest in a 15-story Upper West Side apartment building at 323 West 96th Street to Lightstone Group for approximately $88 million. The transaction generated an $11 million surplus applied to Series C bondholders. Eastdil Secured Savills brokered the deal, which closed in mid-August.
stories.impact: Manhattan's rent-stabilized asset market remains distressed; distressed holders are transferring control to better-capitalized operators. For market-rate developers, this signals subdued acquisition pricing for stabilized rent-regulated buildings in Manhattan, but does not directly affect new supply or multifamily demand. However, Lightstone's acquisition may indicate selective capital returning to Upper West Side residential, where rent regulation limits upside but provides stability.

stories.title: SparrowHawk Buys $400M Midwest Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: SparrowHawk has completed its largest transaction ever, acquiring a 20-property, 4.4 million-square-foot portfolio located across six Midwest logistics markets. The acquisition price was just under $400 million.The assets are in St. Louis, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Dayton and Louisville. The portfolio includes a tenant mix of national and regional companies operating across logistics, distribution, manufacturing, e-commerce, pharmaceutical and related industries. EQT was the seller of the portfolio, and JLL’s Industrial Capital Markets group represented both EQT and SparrowHawk in the transaction. “This acquisition accelerates SparrowHawk’s strategic expansion in the Midwest with a portfolio that is integral to connecting industrial occupiers to the large consumer markets driving logistics and e-commerce growth,” said Alfredo Gutierrez, President and Founder, SparrowHawk. In 2025, SparrowHawk secured approximately $300 million in growth capital through a joint venture with Almanac Realty Investors of New York. SparrowHawk then acquired assets totaling 1.13 million square feet with a combined value of $85 million in Kansas City and St. Louis. The post SparrowHawk Buys $400M Midwest Industrial Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SparrowHawk acquired 4.4M-sf, 20-property Midwest industrial portfolio for $400M from EQT.
Portfolio spans six markets: St. Louis, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Dayton, Louisville.
SparrowHawk secured $300M growth capital via 2025 JV with Almanac; rapid scaling in Midwest.
stories.summary: SparrowHawk completed its largest acquisition ever, purchasing a 20-property, 4.4 million-square-foot industrial portfolio across six Midwest logistics markets (St. Louis, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Dayton, Louisville) from EQT for just under $400 million. The tenant mix spans logistics, distribution, manufacturing, e-commerce, and pharmaceuticals. The deal follows SparrowHawk's $300 million growth capital raise with Almanac Realty Investors in early 2025 and prior acquisitions totaling 1.13 million square feet.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. This signals strong institutional capital flow into Midwest industrial real estate, which may absorb development and debt capital that might otherwise flow to residential. However, robust industrial growth in these six markets (especially St. Louis and Columbus) indicates strong job and logistics hub activity, which could underpin future multifamily demand if residential supply remains constrained.

stories.title: At New York City Council Hearing on Pied-à-Terre Tax, Complaints of a Sloppy Rollout

Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer led the inquiry against what she saw as a dysfunctional rollout of the tax that included publishing up to 900,000 names and addresses of possible second homes in the five boroughs. The Mamdani administration did not send any representatives to the hearing at City Hall, including from the Department of Finance tasked with collecting the tax. The hearing was held by the Committee on Finance and the Committee on Governmental Operations, State and Federal Legislation. “No estimate of the number of pied-à-terres in the city comes even close to 900,000,” Brewer said. “Yet, the city still published the list with the small caveat that the properties on the list may be subject to the charge. The list published by the Department of Finance was so overbroad that it even included my name, and I don’t mind my name and my home address [being included], but I’ve been in that home 365 days a year since 1994. I don’t leave the city, and I don’t have a second home.” The committee hoped to get answers from the Mamdani administration on why — when it had credible information from the New York City Comptroller‘s office about how many second homes there are — it still attempted to force thousands of property owners in the city to prove that the addresses are primary residences. bullets: NYC pied-à-terre tax rollout generated 900,000 flagged property names; City Council scrutiny ongoing.
Department of Finance absent from hearing; overbroad publication of addresses criticized.
Legal battle continues; tax collection uncertainty and administrative dysfunction evident.
stories.summary: The New York City Council held a hearing Tuesday on the controversial pied-à-terre tax surcharge on second homes, with Manhattan Councilmember Gale Brewer leading criticism of a dysfunctional rollout. The Department of Finance published approximately 900,000 property names and addresses as potential pied-à-terre subjects, far exceeding estimates of actual second homes in the city. The Finance Department did not attend the hearing. A legal battle over the tax remains ongoing.
stories.impact: Pied-à-terre tax uncertainty may dampen investor appetite for second-home or speculative residential acquisitions in Manhattan, reducing demand for boutique or luxury rental conversions. However, if the tax ultimately succeeds or expands, it could indirectly boost rental demand as second-home owners liquidate. The administrative chaos and legal risk currently create headwinds for Manhattan multifamily capital deployment and asset valuations tied to speculative buyer pools.

stories.title: Vivmark Residential Launches with $70B Enterprise Value
stories.excerpt: Shares of Vivmark Residential were up Tuesday afternoon following the launch of trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the VMRK ticker. The merger of equals between Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities, creating an apartment REIT with a market capitalization of $51 billion and an enterprise value of $70 billion, was finalized Monday. “Our vision is to be the most trusted and best-performing rental housing company in America and one that gets better as it grows,” said Benjamin Schall, CEO of Vivmark. “Our wider management team of Vivmark officers is now fully in place, and we are ready to deliver a seamless Day 1 experience for our residents.” In addition to Schall, the Vivmark executive team includes Michael Manelis as COO and Kevin O’Shea as CFO. The board includes seven trustees from each company and is led by chairman Stephen Sterrett. Vivmark is dual headquartered in Arlington, VA and Chicago. The post Vivmark Residential Launches with $70B Enterprise Value appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Equity Residential and AvalonBay merger creates Vivmark with $51B market cap, $70B enterprise value.
NYSE listing under VMRK ticker; dual HQ in Arlington, VA and Chicago.
Benjamin Schall CEO; management team fully in place with Michael Manelis (COO) and Kevin O'Shea (CFO).
stories.summary: The merger of equals between Equity Residential and AvalonBay Communities closed Monday, creating Vivmark Residential, a $51 billion market-cap apartment REIT with $70 billion enterprise value. Vivmark began trading on the NYSE under ticker VMRK on Tuesday. Leadership includes CEO Benjamin Schall, COO Michael Manelis, CFO Kevin O'Shea, and a board of 14 trustees split evenly between the legacy companies. Vivmark is dual-headquartered in Arlington, Virginia and Chicago.
stories.impact: This mega-merger consolidates approximately 10% of U.S. apartments into a single platform with enhanced capital, operational scale, and balance-sheet capacity. Vivmark's dual-HQ structure and massive balance sheet signal aggressive competitive positioning in both acquisition and development. Smaller developers should expect intensified competition for development partners, debt, and prime acquisition sites. Vivmark's scale may also lower debt costs relative to mid-tier competitors, pressuring cap rates and making new development feasibility tighter for non-scale players.

stories.title: Irvine Company’s Chicago Office Portfolio 87% Leased Amid Market Momentum
stories.excerpt: Irvine Company announced an increase in leasing activity, bringing its national office portfolio to 91% leased. Irvine Company closed its fiscal year with 11 million square feet of leasing activity, including 4.4 million square feet of new leasing and 6.7 million square feet of renewals. In its Chicago office portfolio, Irvine Company is 87% leased, including activity from financial services and legal services companies. “Our strong leasing activity reflects a clear market trend: companies are actively seeking high-quality environments that bring teams together,” said Roger DeWames, President of Irvine Company Office Properties. “We see continued strong demand for the value and scale we offer, driven by our commitment to continually investing in our premium workplaces and adapting alongside our customers as their business needs change.” Irvine Company completed a new full floor of flex suites at 300 North LaSalle this summer. The move-in-ready workspaces range from 4,500 to 10,000 square feet and offer access to the building’s enterprise amenities. The post Irvine Company’s Chicago Office Portfolio 87% Leased Amid Market Momentum appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Irvine Company Chicago office portfolio 87% leased; national portfolio 91% leased.
FY leasing: 11M sf total activity (4.4M new, 6.7M renewals); strong financial services/legal demand.
Completed flex suites at 300 North LaSalle; premium amenity investment ongoing.
stories.summary: Irvine Company announced strong leasing momentum, with its national office portfolio at 91% leased and its Chicago-specific portfolio at 87% leased. The company closed its fiscal year with 11 million square feet of leasing activity, comprising 4.4 million square feet of new leasing and 6.7 million square feet of renewals. Chicago demand is driven by financial services and legal services tenants. Irvine completed a new full-floor flex suite offering at 300 North LaSalle this summer.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact; this is office sector strength. However, strong Chicago office leasing signals robust job growth and corporate confidence in the market, which can indirectly support apartment demand growth. Irvine's continued investment in premium office amenities indicates capital deployment in downtown Chicago; competing capital demands and potential reduced multifamily development appetite from Irvine in that submarket should be monitored.

stories.title: Albany Road Snags Loan for Scottsdale MOB Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield has arranged $19.9 million in acquisition financing for Edwards Professional Park I & II in Scottsdale. Tyler Morss of Cushman & Wakefield’s Healthcare Capital Markets team arranged the debt through an undisclosed regional bank on behalf of the borrower, Albany Road. Located at 10752 N. 89th Place and 8952 E. Desert Cove Ave., Edwards Professional Park I & II features 91,469 square feet spread across two buildings. At the time of the loan closing, the buildings were currently 91% leased to 47 medical and healthcare-related tenants. Approximately 98.7% of the occupied space is dedicated to healthcare uses, including dentistry, orthopedics, gastroenterology, dermatology, behavioral health, physical medicine, infusion therapy and aesthetic medicine practices. Albany Road has made 110 investments since its inception in 2012 across a wide range of product types, geographies, and tenant profiles. The post Albany Road Snags Loan for Scottsdale MOB Acquisition appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Albany Road secured $19.9M acquisition loan for Edwards Professional Park (medical office) in Scottsdale.
91,469 sf across two buildings; 91% leased to 47 healthcare tenants at closing.
98.7% of occupied space healthcare-dedicated (dentistry, orthopedics, gastroenterology, dermatology, etc.).
stories.summary: Cushman & Wakefield arranged $19.9 million in acquisition financing for Albany Road to purchase Edwards Professional Park I & II in Scottsdale. The two-building, 91,469-square-foot medical office complex was 91% leased to 47 healthcare providers at loan closing, with 98.7% of occupied space dedicated to healthcare services including dentistry, orthopedics, gastroenterology, dermatology, behavioral health, and infusion therapy.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. MOB financing remains active and available in Scottsdale, but capital deployed to healthcare real estate is capital not deployed to multifamily. The deal signals confidence in Scottsdale's healthcare infrastructure and population base, which can support apartment demand long-term; however, competitive capital positioning for medical office may constrain multifamily construction financing availability in the Phoenix MSA.

stories.title: Betting on South Beach Luxury Shopping, Vivienne Westwood Plans to Open Store
stories.excerpt: Vivienne Westwood is finally getting serious about opening a boutique in Miami’s South Beach. Almost two years after buying the three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue and letting it sit vacant, the luxury fashion brand has submitted an application to build out the property, which dates back to 1921. The 4,356-square-foot ground-floor space would feature a store with three fittings rooms and two storage rooms. The second floor would house executive offices and meeting rooms, while the top floor would include a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. A neon sign would be mounted onto the entrance wall. The project “honors the building’s 1921 Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival heritage while introducing contemporary elements,” wrote Daniel Gabay, who runs National Permit Group and filed the proposal. The modern elements include “Florida limestone cladding, polished brass storefront and motifs, a rigid canopy reinterpreting the documented historic faux eave, a landmark pink neon signature, and the iconic Orb statue in the forecourt,” per the application, which Miami Beach Historic Preservation Board will consider next month. In 2024, the British brand paid $6 million for the 14,692-square-foot building located just a few blocks west of Ocean Drive, sandwiched between Seventh and Eighth Streets. Unlike most luxury labels of its size, it remains independent under the ownership of Vivienne Westwood’s family. The namesake designer passed away in 2022. Vivienne Westwood, the brand, is betting that high-end retail will return to the heart of South Beach. In the 1990s and 2000s, the area housed boutiques from the likes of Versace, Hugo Boss and Barney’s. But almost all shuttered, opting instead to open outposts at the Bal Harbour Shops up north and the Design District out west, which have become some of the highest-grossing upscale malls in the country. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Vivienne Westwood submitted buildout application for 736 Collins Avenue, South Beach Miami.
4,356 sf ground floor retail; second floor offices; third floor bridal showroom and rooftop deck.

stories.summary: Luxury fashion brand Vivienne Westwood, which purchased the three-story property at 736 Collins Avenue in South Beach, Miami nearly two years ago, has submitted a building permit application for buildout. The 4,356-square-foot ground floor will feature a boutique with fitting rooms; the second floor will include executive offices; the third floor will house a bridal showroom and rooftop deck. The project restores the 1921 Art Deco and Mediterranean Revival architecture with contemporary finishes including limestone cladding and a pink neon signature.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. This signals retail/luxury tenant confidence and capital deployment in South Beach, which indicates sustained demand for premium experiential retail and suggests the neighborhood remains attractive to high-end brands. However, extended vacancy (nearly two years) before buildout may indicate tenancy challenges or capital constraints in South Beach retail, which could affect mixed-use development feasibility in the submarket.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Vickey Barron of Compass
stories.excerpt: Vickey Barron, an associate broker at Compass, knows how to get deals done — and all with the perfect mix of intelligence, charm, charisma and a take-no-nonsense attitude. It’s what makes her one of the best real estate brokers in the business. Barron, 69, has worked on more than 600 sales during her career and earned a slew of awards, including the Real Estate Board of New York’s Rookie of the Year award in 2001 and the board’s Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award in 2015. Barron has done an endless amount of million-dollar deals, but for her, the value of her job isn’t money — it’s the difference she can make in someone’s life. “People always want me to talk about commissions and big sales, and I just am a strong believer that our purpose in this role of real estate is not money and commission and who has the biggest numbers,” Barron said. “It’s really about serving people.” Commercial Observer caught up with Barron in August for a new series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What was the biggest deal of your career? Vickey Barron: Ironically, this is not the one with the highest sale price or largest commission. In our business, there tends to be an emphasis on the commissions and money earned, but, going back to basics, we are in the business of helping people find homes and find solace. My biggest and most important deal was helping a 93-year-old woman negotiate a life estate so she could remain in her West Village townhouse after the sale took place. Sometimes we get caught up and forget that we’re all human and we age. Life has chapters, and our contributions matter. This deal had the biggest and most positive impact in my career. bullets: Profile: Vickey Barron, Compass associate broker, 69, 600+ sales career.
Awards: REBNY Rookie of the Year (2001), Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award (2015).
Philosophy: values people and service over commissions and deal size.
stories.summary: Commercial Observer profiled Vickey Barron, a 69-year-old associate broker at Compass with over 600 sales during her career. Barron has earned multiple awards including the Real Estate Board of New York's Rookie of the Year (2001) and Eileen Spinola Distinguished Service Award (2015). She emphasizes service and human impact over commissions and deal volume in her real estate practice.
stories.impact: No material impact on multifamily development. This is a human-interest profile of a brokerage professional; no market signals, capital flows, supply, demand, or cost implications.

stories.title: Green Street Expands Student Housing Data Platform
stories.excerpt: Investors eyeing student housing assets have a newly expanded study tool. College House, a destination for specialized data and analytics on the U.S. student housing sector, is officially offering investors and operators direct access to analytics firm Green Street’s investment analytics. The platform expansion launched on Tuesday, a little more than a year after Green Street acquired College House in 2025. The news comes amid a complicated cooling period for the U.S. student housing market, according to Green Street’s own 2026 student housing report. Asset values have declined recently due to rising cap rates, while revenue growth is expected to average just 2 percent over the next two years, slightly trailing apartments. Capital is returning to student housing, according to commercial real estate finance firm Walker & Dunlop’s annual outlook, but is similarly selective, and activity remains below 2022 peaks. Construction starts are slowing and deliveries are highly concentrated, with the market splitting along enrollment trends. College House users can now tap Green Street estimates tailored to the student housing market within its platform, including key metrics like cap rates, risk-adjusted return estimates, occupancy and supply. The announcement also introduced a proprietary scoring framework, dubbed University Grades, that identifies long-term rent growth potential for nearly 180 U.S. schools. “This is exactly the integration we envisioned when we acquired College House,” Andrew McCulloch, chief analytics officer of Green Street, said in a statement. “Combining Green Street’s independent research and proprietary valuation framework with College House’s best-in-class data assets, will provide student housing investors a complete toolkit to allocate capital more effectively.” Time for investors to hit the books. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Green Street expanded College House platform; direct access to Green Street investment analytics.
Expansion launched Tuesday, over one year after Green Street acquired College House in 2025.
Student housing market cooling: cap rates rising, asset values declining, revenue growth ~2% over 2 years.
stories.summary: College House, a specialized student housing data and analytics platform, officially launched direct access to Green Street's investment analytics on Tuesday, more than a year after Green Street's 2025 acquisition. The expansion provides investors and operators enhanced underwriting and market intelligence. However, Green Street's own 2026 student housing report describes a cooling market: asset values have declined due to rising cap rates, and revenue growth is expected to average just 2 percent over the next two years, tracking slightly below apartment sector growth. Capital is returning but remains selective, with activity still below 2022 peaks.
stories.impact: Student housing is a specialized multifamily asset class facing structural headwinds: rising cap rates, modest revenue growth (2% vs. apartments), and selective capital redeployment. For multifamily developers, this signals risk in student housing development starts and refinancing; capital discipline required. However, the gap between student housing (2% growth) and broader apartments suggests traditional Class A and workforce multifamily face tighter underwriting but stronger relative fundamentals. Developers should avoid student housing starts in weaker college towns and focus on core multifamily markets.
